title: A ':60' leap-second timestamp raises in Python, is an Invalid Date in JS -- and V8's fallback parser silently turns it into 23:59:00
assumption: A timestamp string like 2016-12-31T23:59:60Z, which is how official leap-second records are written, is a value your date library can parse.

input.display: "2016-12-31T23:59:60Z" (the real UTC leap second inserted at the end of 2016)
input.description: Parsing a timestamp from an NTP/GPS log, a scientific instrument feed, or any system that records UTC leap seconds literally in its output, where one legitimately occurred (e.g. 2016-12-31 23:59:60 UTC).

what_goes_wrong: Feeding a real, historically-occurring leap-second timestamp to a standard date parser fails three different ways: loudly in Python, as a silently invalid Date for an ISO string in JavaScript, and, for a non-ISO string in V8 (Node, Chrome), as a valid-looking time one minute too early.
why: Python's `datetime` and the ECMAScript date-time string format both model a minute as seconds 00 through 59, with no slot for the 61st second a leap second inserts. In Python, `datetime(..., second=60)`, `datetime.strptime` and `datetime.fromisoformat` all raise `ValueError` (the older `time.strptime`, by contrast, accepts 60). ECMA-262 requires `Date.parse` to return `NaN` for a string in its ISO format with an out-of-bounds field, so `"2016-12-31T23:59:60Z"` yields an Invalid Date: no exception, every <, >, <=, >= comparison with it is false, and `.toISOString()` throws `RangeError` only later, at the point of use. Strings outside the ISO format go to implementation-defined fallback parsing, and there V8 accepts `"Sat, 31 Dec 2016 23:59:60 GMT"` and returns 2016-12-31T23:59:00Z -- a valid Date 60 seconds early, with no error at all. Other engines may differ, since that fallback is not specified.

repros.expected_output: ValueError at construction: second must be in 0..59, not 60

Date.parse result: NaN isNaN: true
Date object: Invalid Date | valid: false
V8 fallback parse of RFC 2822 ':60': 2016-12-31T23:59:00.000Z

fix: Never parse a raw leap-second timestamp with the standard date constructor. Detect `:60` (or `:59.999...` smeared variants, depending on the source) before parsing and either clamp it to `:59` with a documented policy or route it through a library that explicitly models leap seconds (e.g. one backed by TAI); and in JavaScript, always check `Number.isNaN(date.getTime())` immediately after any `Date.parse`/`new Date(string)` rather than trusting the object; and never hand a non-ISO timestamp string to `new Date()` / `Date.parse`, whose fallback parsing is engine-specific.

sources.title: IETF RFC 3339: Date and Time on the Internet (leap seconds)
ECMA-262: Date.parse (non-ISO strings are implementation-defined; out-of-bounds ISO fields return NaN)
